before: object-fit controls how an image’s contents fit its own box. contain shows the whole image with unused space; cover fills the box and may crop.

The HTML supplies the elements; CSS supplies their presentation. This small fixture uses horizontal writing and left-to-right direction. ```html
``` ```css .demo { writing-mode: horizontal-tb; direction: ltr; } .photo { display: block; width: 100px; height: 100px; object-fit: contain; object-position: center; background: navy; } ```

The img is an HTML element, not a function. .photo selects its class. width and height make a square element box. object-fit: contain preserves the image’s 2:1 natural ratio inside that box. object-position: center centers the fitted contents.

Use contain when all of a diagram must be visible; use cover when a crop is acceptable. Neither choice changes alt text. Our original inline SVG needs no external asset. The box stays square in both cases.
Show the full original image in a centered square without stretching it.
after: An image has its own contents and an element box around them. `object-fit` chooses how the picture fits inside that box. `contain` shows the whole picture. `cover` fills the box but can cut off part of the picture.
The supplied picture is twice as wide as it is tall. `contain` keeps that proportion, so the picture is not stretched into a square. `object-position: center` centers the picture inside the box.
With `cover`, this wide picture would fill the square and lose parts at the sides. The element box would still be 100 by 100 pixels. The change affects how the picture fits inside it.

Use `contain` when the whole diagram or picture matters. Use `cover` when a crop is acceptable. Neither setting changes the image’s `alt` text, which gives a written replacement for its useful information.
Keep the supplied picture and its description. Show it centered inside the square with `contain`. Run the checks and make sure the whole picture is visible.
